newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Diplomats meet Serbian opposition over local elex.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats meet Serbian opposition over local elex.

text.p: Leaders of Serbia's opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition met western diplomats on Monday as demonstrations against the government's attempt to annul local election results entered their eighth day.
Ambassadors from several Western embassies held talks with Zajedno leaders after meeting Yugoslav foreign minister Milan Milutinovic over the weekend.

The Socialists at first conceded they had lost councils in Belgrade and industrial towns across Serbia, but electoral commissions under their control later claimed to have found unspecified irregularities and called a third round of voting.
Zajedno urged a boycott of the third round in Belgrade and other key towns where they say they were cheated of legal victories.

Although diplomatic sources confirmed that the ambassadors' meetings with both Milutinovic and Zajedno discussed the growing crisis surrounding the election results, they maintained a disciplined silence over the diplomats' message.
One Western source said Zajedno outlined the legal steps they planned to use to challenge the Socialists' tactics.
A Zajedno statement declared the decision to annul the results was "the greatest nullification of elections since Yugoslavia was created in 1918".
"Legal methods used for the nullification of election results... show that the regime is unscrupulous, has a total control over judicial bodies and totally ignores the laws of Yugoslavia," it said.

Western countries, including the United States, Britain and France, have expressed dismay at the way the ruling Socialist Party of President Slobodan Milosevic handled the elections which gave an unexpected victory to Zajedno in most major towns.
But they have so far offered only muted statements of concern over possible election fraud.
Opposition leaders have appealed for international support, which they said could tip the balance in their favour.
The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting war in former Yugoslavia.
But they now view him as a guarantor of Balkan peace after he signed a U.S.- brokered peace treaty last year and may wish to avoid an open confrontation with him.
Western countries do have indirect weapons they can use.

These could include adding fairness in elections to existing stipulations - such as a peaceful solution of the Kosovo issue and compliance with the peace process in Bosnia - as the price for normalising international relations with Yugoslavia.
As the ambassadors discussed the crisis with Zajedno leaders, opposition supporters continued to express their frustration by staging an eighth day of protests in the capital.
At least 5,000 students including police academy recruits marched into the city centre to join a growing Zajedno demonstration that one local radio station estimated to be about 100,000 strong.
